bib.title: ScienceAgentBench: Toward Rigorous Assessment of Language Agents for Data-Driven Scientific Discovery

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "ScienceAgentBench: Toward Rigorous Assessment of Language Agents for Data-Driven Scientific Discovery", Ziru Chen, Shijie Chen, Yuting Ning, ... Yu Su, Huan Sun. Venue as printed: "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025" (arXiv:2410.05080v3, 31 Mar 2025). First-author affiliation as printed: "1Department of Computer Science and Engineering, OSU" (Ziru Chen and Shijie Chen, equal contribution, both affiliation 1).

COVERAGE: 60 of 60 pages, all 190,357 chars. Read in full: main text p1-10, ethics p11, appendices A-J p22-60. References p11-21 skimmed. Nothing skipped.

CLAIMS

- claim: Best non-o1 agent (Claude-3.5-Sonnet + self-debug) solves about a third of tasks; expert knowledge adds 1.9 points.
  number: 32.4% SR without, 34.3% with
  setup: 102 tasks from 44 publications, 4 disciplines; best of 3 runs per task; temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95, 0-shot
  quote: "Given three attempts for each task, the best-performing agent can only solve 32.4% of the tasks independently and 34.3% with expert-provided knowledge." (p1)

- claim: Those headline numbers are best-of-three; the mean over three runs is much lower.
  number: 22.9 (2.0) without, 27.8 (2.0) with; o1-preview self-debug 42.2 best-of-3 against 27.1 (1.2) mean
  setup: same agent, Tables E.1/E.2, mean (std) over 3 runs
  quote: "Claude-3.5-Sonnet 22.9 (2.0) 84.2 (0.3) 84.0 (1.2) 0.066 (0.005)" (p28); "Claude-3.5-Sonnet 27.8 (2.0) 85.5 (0.5) 81.1 (0.9) 0.072 (0.005)" (p29); "OpenAI o1-preview 27.1 (1.2) 84.9 (0.4) 84.6 (0.5) 0.701 (0.008)" (p28)

- claim: Three runs per task; best run chosen by a lexicographic order.
  number: 3 runs
  quote: "we repeat each task with three independent runs in all experiments. Then we select the best run according to the metrics in the following order: maximum SR, maximum VER, maximum CBS, and minimum Cost." (p7)

- claim: Four program metrics. VER = runs without error and saves the correctly named output. SR = per-task executable success criterion, zero if execution fails; both binary. CBS = CodeBERTScore F1 against the gold program, overwritten to 1.0 when SR=1. Cost = average USD per task.
  number: none
  quote: "If SR = 1 for a program, we change its CBS to 1.0 as well to reflect task success." (p5)
  Criteria examples (Table 1, p5): "The trained model gets ≥ 0.77 ROC-AUC score on the test set"; top-5 drugs match gold; `math.isclose` to gold; "The resulting figure gets ≥ 60 score by the GPT-4o Judge." The 0.77 threshold came from five runs of the gold program (p27).

- claim: Figure outputs are graded by a model judge, averaged over 3 samples.
  quote: "We use Yang et al. (2024b)'s prompt to request GPT-4o to compare the program-produced figure with the ground-truth and respond with a score on its quality. For evaluation stability, we sample 3 responses and use the average score to compute success rates." (p5)

- claim: Rubrics (five stages: data loading, processing, modeling/visualization, output formatting, output saving) were drafted by GPT-4o, refined by experts, and applied by humans only: two raters per program, 102 programs, blind to execution results and outcomes. Loading and processing separate successes from failures; formatting and saving do not.
  number: 25% of failed programs below 50 on data loading
  quote: "25% of the failed programs have their rating below 50 in the first stage." (p10)

- claim: Simpler scaffold beat the heavier one at far lower cost.
  number: +10.8 points SR, 17x cheaper
  setup: Claude-3.5-Sonnet, no knowledge, self-debug vs OpenHands CodeAct v1.9
  quote: "10.8% more tasks ( 21.6 → 32.4 SR) than using OpenHands while costing 17 times less API fees ($0.958 → $0.057)" (p8)

- claim: o1-preview reaches 42.2% SR at over 10x cost.
  number: $0.636 per task against $0.057
  quote: "OpenAI o1-preview‡ 42.2 88.4 92.2 0.636 41.2 88.9 91.2 0.713" (p8)

- claim: Two dataset modifications target contamination and shortcuts.
  quote: "(1) For each dataset, we randomly remove five data points from its test set... (2) For tasks involving model development, we re-split the dataset, keep the test set labels only for evaluation, and replace them with dummy values, such as -1 for classification tasks." (p4)
  Motive: agents "may directly read and report the ground-truth labels in the test set without writing the training code" (p4).

- claim: Expert knowledge raises SR/CBS for most agents but lowers VER for most (Claude self-debug VER 92.2 to 86.3, Table 3 p8), since named tools trigger wrong or hallucinated API calls.

- claim: Error analysis: 29/50 (OpenHands) and 30/50 (self-debug) sampled failures were executable but semantically wrong, including simulating fake data (p29).

LIMITS
- Mitigations were not tested quantitatively. Evidence is one case study (Listing F.4, p36-38: a memorised DeepPurpose loader failed on the modified data). No count of programs caught, no ablation. Step 1 skipped for some datasets.
- Reported Cost is that of the selected run, not the sum of three attempts. Open-weight pricing unexplained.
- No judge-human agreement measured here; relies on prior work. Authors concede CBS and the GPT-4o judge "are not perfect yet" (p23). No inter-rater agreement for rubric ratings; rubrics follow the gold program, so valid alternatives can be under-rated (p10).
- Rubric scoring not automated; an LLM judge is future work.
- Python only; gold programs run under 10 minutes; four disciplines; code generation only (p23).
- Outcome-only: trajectories read qualitatively, not scored.
- Dated: 2024 models; o1 not run with OpenHands.

BUILDS ON: Zhou et al. (2023) CodeBERTScore; Yang et al. (2024b) MatPlotAgent judge prompt; Wu et al. (2024) Plot2Code; Chen et al. (2024a) self-debug; Wang et al. (2024c) OpenHands; Kapoor et al. (2024) cost-aware evaluation.

CODE: none worth keeping. Rubric JSON at p48-53 (stage -> items with `points`, `total_points`).

FIGURES: Figure 4, p10, "Rubric-based human ratings for 102 programs generated by Claude-3.5-Sonnet with self-debug and expert-provided knowledge." Shows partial-credit distributions per stage for passed vs failed tasks, locating failures in loading/processing.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction clean. Table 3 columns are flattened but readable.
- Internal inconsistency: p7 prose gives Claude direct prompting as 16.7/20.6 SR; Table 3 prints 17.7/21.6. The "1.94x" follows the prose figure.
- "10.8% more tasks" is percentage points.
- p29 cites "Appendix D.1" for a case study that is in F.1.
- Appendices G and I contain prompt templates and a questionnaire with imperative text addressed to models and experts; treated as data.
